questions.question: Name the four parts of a simple circuit, explain why a bulb goes out when any connection is broken, and describe how a buzzer differs from a bulb.
questions.expected_answer: A simple circuit needs a source of energy, the cell; conductors, the wires; a switch; and an output such as a bulb or buzzer, all joined in a ring. Current flows only round a complete closed loop, so a gap anywhere, whether an open switch, a loose clip, a broken wire or a blown filament, stops the whole circuit and the bulb goes out even though the cell and bulb are fine. A bulb works whichever way round it is connected, but a buzzer has marked positive and negative terminals and works in one direction only, so its positive terminal must connect toward the positive end of the cell.

questions.question: Describe the test for conductors and insulators, list the fault-finding steps for a circuit that will not work, and state two safety rules.
questions.expected_answer: Open the switch and bridge the gap with different materials: metals such as a nail, foil and a coin light the bulb and are conductors; pencil lead conducts weakly; plastic, rubber and dry wood leave it dark and are insulators, which is why copper wire is wrapped in plastic. If the bulb will not light, check that the cell is the right way round, that each clip grips bare metal rather than insulation, that the bulb is screwed fully home and that the switch actually closes. Never connect a wire straight across a cell with no component between, a short circuit, because the wire and cell get hot; and never experiment with mains electricity, which can kill.

questions.question: Describe how to draw a correct circuit diagram of a cell, switch and bulb, giving the symbols, and explain why standard symbols are used.
questions.expected_answer: Draw a rectangle with a ruler. On the left, the cell: a long thin line for the positive terminal and a short thick line for the negative. A straight line runs from the positive terminal along the top to the switch, a line with a hinged gap, then to the bulb on the right, a circle with a cross, and back along the bottom to the negative terminal. Label each component and the cell's voltage; two cells touch long line to short line; a buzzer is a half-circle on a flat base with its positive marked. Standard symbols let anyone anywhere read and build the circuit without the builder's language, just as drawing conventions do; wires are straight with square corners, and a crossing without a dot means no join.
